title: Crisis protection is becoming a capability problem: systems must scale up temporarily and scale down credibly
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11454, Get Ready: What Lessons for Social Protection from the Recent Energy Crisis?
geography: Global country-response review covering the March-May 2026 energy crisis, with comparisons to responses during the 2008, 2020, and 2022 crises

observations.period: March-May 2026; global energy-crisis policy response tracker

denominator.unit: countries with planned or implemented social-policy responses as of May 7, 2026

global_reach.value: about half of countries worldwide had planned or implemented a response

response_heterogeneity.value: actions varied with crisis interpretation, price transmission, fiscal space, and interaction with monetary policy

mechanism.value: uncertain shock duration makes governments hesitate between immediate relief, inflation control, and preparedness for persistent volatility

observations.method: Descriptive global coding of country responses in 2026, compared with response patterns during earlier economic and price crises.
observations.uncertainty: The tracker records announced, planned, or implemented policy actions, not uniform spending, coverage, household receipt, price effects, or welfare outcomes; timing and classification can change as the crisis evolves.
observations.subgroup: Countries with different income levels, fiscal space, inflation conditions, administrative systems, energy exposure, and political incentives; households and firms exposed differently to energy-price transmission.
observations.counterinterpretation: Non-response can reflect limited local inflation or fiscal constraints rather than weak protection capacity, while a large response count can conceal shallow, delayed, or poorly targeted implementation.

denominator.unit: global social-policy responses recorded as of May 7, 2026

subsidy_position.value: subsidies accounted for nearly half of current responses

historical_comparison.value: from 2022 through 2026, the share of subsidies among crisis responses was more than three times the share of cash transfers

political_logic.value: subsidies can be introduced quickly, suppress visible price increases, support selected sectors, and appear more scalable than alternatives even when they are fiscally costly

consumer_translation.value: the policy instrument changes whether relief appears as a lower price, a transfer, a service, or a less visible future fiscal burden

observations.method: Cross-crisis descriptive comparison of classified social-assistance, subsidy, labor-market, insurance, service, and preparedness responses.
observations.uncertainty: Instrument shares do not establish which response protected households best; subsidies may stabilize prices or sectors while benefiting groups unevenly and weakening fiscal room for later protection.
observations.subgroup: Energy consumers, firms, sectors, taxpayers, cash-transfer recipients, informal households, and groups with different ability to absorb inflation or access administrative systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cash transfers may be more distributionally efficient in theory but slower or harder to deliver where registries, payment systems, trust, or fiscal space are weak; subsidies can have non-income objectives such as price containment or energy security.

denominator.unit: illustrative reform scenarios for making social protection more crisis ready

scalability_rule.value: prepare seriously, scale up temporarily, and scale down credibly

institutional_requirement.value: crisis response requires pre-agreed triggers, delivery infrastructure, financing, communication, and a credible exit path rather than improvisation after prices rise

legitimacy_test.value: temporary protection is politically durable only if households can understand eligibility, receive support in time, and believe withdrawal rules are predictable rather than arbitrary

open_outcome.value: the paper proposes reform scenarios and a framework, not a causal evaluation of household welfare or trust

observations.method: Conceptual crisis-response framework and four illustrative reform scenarios grounded in comparative policy tracking.
observations.uncertainty: The scenarios are design propositions; their effectiveness depends on country-specific administrative capacity, fiscal rules, political coalitions, shock duration, and household take-up.
observations.subgroup: Existing beneficiaries, newly exposed households, people outside registries, workers and firms affected by price transmission, and taxpayers funding temporary expansion.
observations.counterinterpretation: Automatic triggers and exit rules can improve credibility but may be too rigid for shocks that change in composition, or may withdraw support before households regain income and service stability.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank document page for WPS11454 and its subject metadata.
Bibliographic record and abstract for WPS11454.
Author-authored contemporaneous summary of the response tracker, subsidy dominance, fiscal constraints, and crisis-insurance framing.
Related World Bank/ILO tracker covering 195 countries, 3,842 data points, and five social-policy categories.

boundary: This record adds crisis scalability and policy-instrument choice as a social-protection, household-cost, and legitimacy mechanism. It does not estimate household welfare, receipt, poverty reduction, trust, or causal protection effects, and it does not establish that subsidies are always inferior to transfers or that automatic triggers work equally across countries.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, official document page, abstract record, author summary, and related tracker metadata were reviewed for the 2026 response count, country coverage, policy mix, historical comparison, crisis-response framework, four reform scenarios, and evidence boundaries.
